Ask before photographing people - especially women and families - and never photograph government buildings, military sites, airports' secure areas or anyone praying up close. Devote a day to Al-Balad, Jeddah's UNESCO-listed old town: coral-stone merchant houses with carved wooden roshan balconies, souqs that have traded since the port served pilgrims centuries ago, and coffee houses tucked into restored courtyards. The second day belongs to the Red Sea - a boat trip or a snorkel over reefs that are among the least dived in the region, then the Corniche again at golden hour to see King Fahd's Fountain, one of the tallest of its kind in the world. If you are travelling in the hotter months and have a spare day, the mountain city of Taif, a few hours inland, is the traditional summer escape: cooler air, roses and roadside fruit stalls.

Dress modestly in public: shoulders and knees covered is a good working rule for everyone. Women are not required to wear an abaya or cover their hair as tourists - that rule changed years ago - but loose, modest clothing is both respectful and simply more comfortable. Swimwear belongs at the beach and pool; the Red Sea resorts operate much like resorts anywhere. At religious sites, stricter dress applies and women cover their hair to enter mosque areas.

Drive if you want to - women have held Saudi licences since 2018 and rental desks treat a woman driver as unremarkable. The Kingdom rewards the same approach as anywhere: dress with the place in mind, learn five words of Arabic, and go.

Drive the escarpment road up from the Red Sea coast and the temperature falls away. Abha, capital of the Asir region, sits above 2,200 metres; the peaks around Al Soudah pass 3,000 metres - the highest ground in Saudi Arabia. Summer here brings cloud, drizzle and green terraces while Riyadh sits in the high forties, which is why Saudis themselves holiday in Asir. If your picture of the Kingdom is only desert, this is the region that corrects it.

During Ramadan the rhythm inverts: days are quiet, and after sunset the cities celebrate. Eating in public during fasting hours is discreetly avoided by visitors out of respect, though hotels serve non-fasting guests.

During Ramadan, Saudi Arabia inverts its day. From dawn to sunset, Muslims fast; offices and many shops run shorter hours, cities feel hushed by afternoon — and then, at the maghrib call to prayer, everything ignites. Iftar, the fast-breaking meal, turns restaurants, tents and family homes into the centre of the world, and the streets stay alive past midnight, past 2am, sometimes until the pre-dawn suhoor meal.

During the Eid breaks, government offices close - and that includes the machinery behind visas and embassies. Applications in progress pause, official counters reopen afterwards, and the working days on either side run at half pace. If your trip is fixed, apply well clear of an Eid week rather than against it; our processing time guide explains how weekends already shape timings, and Eid stretches the same effect over most of a week. Banks and many private businesses close or shorten hours too, while malls, restaurants and attractions typically do the opposite, opening late and celebrating.

Eid dates follow the Hijri lunar calendar, so they arrive roughly eleven days earlier each Gregorian year, and the exact day is confirmed by the sighting of the new moon close to the time - which is why any website that states an Eid date years ahead 'definitively' is guessing. Public holidays around each Eid run for several days, longer for government employees. Our Hijri converter turns any Gregorian date into its Hijri equivalent and back, which is the practical tool for trip planning: pick your travel dates, see where they fall in the Islamic year, and you will know whether an Eid is likely to overlap.

First-time visitors are fingerprinted and photographed at passport control; it takes under a minute

First-timers do well in Olaya and the King Abdullah Financial District for business polish, or near Tahlia Street for restaurants and evening life. Food is one of Riyadh's pleasures: Saudi kabsa and jareesh for the traditional table, and one of the Middle East's deepest international restaurant scenes around them. Coffee is a culture of its own - specialty coffee bars are everywhere and stay open late, which is when the city does much of its socialising.
Fitting the week to your visa

Five times a day the country breathes in: mosques fill, some smaller shops close briefly, and meetings pause. It lasts minutes, not hours, and the correct response is simply patience - wait, have a coffee, let it pass. In Ramadan the rhythm deepens: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, eating and drinking in public during the day is impolite (and in some settings restricted), and the evenings come alive with iftar meals you may well be invited to. Accept - it is one of the great travel experiences the Kingdom offers.

Five times a day, life briefly pauses for prayer. Shops may close for a short period around prayer times, especially in smaller towns, and Friday is the week's holy day - many businesses open later, after Friday prayers. Plan around it loosely and it never becomes a problem: attractions list their prayer-time closures, and the pause is a good excuse for coffee.

For Muslim pilgrims travelling for Umrah: how you reach Makkah, where to stay, how the Haramain train changes the journey, and how to pace your days around the prayers. Makkah is open to Muslims only.

For Muslim travellers, the natural finale is Umrah: the Haramain high-speed train runs from Jeddah to Makkah in under an hour, and Umrah can be performed on a tourist visa outside the Hajj period - arrange the Nusuk permit before you travel, and read our Makkah guide before you go. Makkah itself is open to Muslims only, so other travellers should give the day to Madinah instead, or simply slow down in Jeddah. Non-Muslim visitors may enter Madinah, though the sanctuary area immediately around the Prophet's Mosque is reserved for Muslim worshippers; the city's museums, markets and Mount Uhud viewpoint make a full and moving day regardless.

For Muslim visitors, prayer in the Prophet's Mosque is the heart of the trip, and the Rawdah - the small, carpeted area between the Prophet's chamber and the pulpit, described in hadith as a garden of Paradise - is its most sought-after corner. Access to the Rawdah is by timed permit booked in the Nusuk app, and slots go quickly: book as soon as your dates are fixed, arrive early, and expect a short, moving, tightly organised visit.

For men the code is shorter. Trousers or long shorts below the knee in the cities, shirts or t-shirts with sleeves, and nothing with offensive slogans or images. The two firm lines: no sleeveless vests in public, and swimwear belongs at the beach or pool, not the street. For business meetings, dress a level up - a suit or smart trousers and a collared shirt match the room, and Saudi counterparts are usually impeccably turned out. Traditional white thobes are for Saudis; visitors are not expected to wear one, and buying a ghutra as a costume will read as exactly that.

For most of the country, this is the window: Riyadh in the low-to-mid 20s by day, Jeddah warm and humid-mild, AlUla's desert cool enough for all-day exploring and cold at night. It is also peak season - Riyadh Season and Diriyah Season run, AlUla's Winter at Tantora festival lands, flights and hotels price accordingly, and the best desert camps book out. If your dates are flexible inside the season, the edges (early November, late February) give you the weather with slightly thinner crowds.

For most of the twentieth century the Kingdom's story was oil - discovered at Dammam in 1938 and still central to the economy. The twenty-first century story is diversification: under Saudi Vision 2030 the country has opened to tourism, entertainment, sport and foreign business at a pace few expected, and the tourist eVisa launched in 2019 was one of the first doors to swing open.

For most visitors, yes - Saudi Arabia is a safe country to travel in, and it feels that way quickly. Street crime and theft against tourists are uncommon, cities are well lit and busy late into the evening, and families think nothing of being out in parks and corniches after dark. The honest risks are different from the ones people imagine: the road traffic, the summer heat, and the possibility of breaking a law you did not know existed. All three are manageable with a little preparation, which is what this guide is for.

For the standard tourist eVisa, no confirmed hotel booking or flight ticket is required at application stage. Sponsored visit visas and transit visas have their own requirements - a transit visa is issued with your Saudia or flynas ticket.

For the tourist eVisa the set is the same as for adults: the child's passport and a recent photograph on a white background - the photo rules apply in full, and children's photos are a common cause of avoidable delay. Sponsored family visit visas ask for more: proof of the relationship to the host, such as a birth certificate, is the document that matters there, translated if it is not in Arabic or English.

For visitors from eligible countries, the eVisa moved the whole transaction online: apply from home, receive a digital visa by email, print it or carry it on your phone, and present it with the passport it was issued against. No appointment, no surrendered passport, no sticker. The border officer sees the same record either way - the difference is entirely in how the visa reaches you and how much of your life it interrupts first.
Foreign women are not legally required to wear an abaya or a headscarf in public

Foreign women are not legally required to wear an abaya, and have not been since the Kingdom opened to tourism in 2019. A headscarf is likewise not required in public - the exception is inside mosques, covered below. In practice, dress sits on a spectrum by place: in Jeddah and Riyadh's modern districts, long dresses, wide trousers and loose tops are unremarkable, while in Madinah, Qassim and smaller towns, most visitors choose an abaya because everyone around them is wearing one and it is the easiest way to feel comfortable. An abaya is also genuinely useful kit: it goes over anything, solves every 'is this modest enough' question, and packs to nothing. Many first-time visitors buy one on arrival and wonder why they hesitated.
Founding Day is 22 February and National Day is 23 September, both fixed

Four days is enough for the classic first taste: Diriyah and old Riyadh from the capital's airport, or Al-Balad and the Corniche from Jeddah. Many travellers use the stopover for Umrah - it is permitted outside the Hajj season, with Umrah and Rawdah slots booked in the Nusuk app.

Give Al-Balad a slow morning or a golden late afternoon. Its tower houses were built from Red Sea coral stone and teak, fronted with rawashin - the enclosed wooden lattice balconies that catch the sea breeze and shade the streets. Naseef House, the old merchant mansion turned museum, anchors the visit; around it, the souqs sell everything from oud and textiles to gold, and the lanes keep revealing carved doors. Restoration is ongoing and serious - parts feel like a building site in the best sense, a heritage district being handed back to the city.

Give the capital two days and a plan: the National Museum for the story, Masmak Fortress and the old souqs for the roots, Kingdom Centre's Sky Bridge for the grid of the modern city at dusk, and Boulevard City if your trip lands in Riyadh Season. The new metro has quietly made crossing the city painless. Riyadh rewards structure - its sights are spread across a big, working capital, not gathered in one old town.
Give the mosque more than one visit at different hours. Dawn, when the umbrellas unfold and the courtyard fills with soft light, is the Madinah moment most people carry home.

Hegra first, early in the day - the tombs of Qasr al-Farid and the Banat cluster are best in morning light and before the heat, and entry runs on timed tours booked in advance. Hold a passport that meets the validity requirement for your route, and check your details on anything we send you for review

Hold a valid visit visa for the US, the UK or a Schengen state, and have actually travelled on it at least once? You are assessed for a Saudi visa on arrival. The 'used once' condition is the whole ballgame - a fresh, unused visa opens nothing. Because the final decision happens at the border, treat this as a real route but not a risk-free one, and have your documents in order before you fly.

Holders can be assessed on arrival at Saudi international airports, where the visa is issued at the border - workable, but it puts the decision at the end of a flight, in a queue, with your whole trip depending on it. The calmer option is applying for the eVisa in advance through the same route: the assessment happens before you travel, and you board the plane with the visa already issued.

Holders of a Saudi tourist eVisa can perform Umrah for most of the year. The two conditions are timing and permit: Umrah is not performed on a tourist visa during the Hajj season, and you book your Umrah and Rawdah time slots through the Nusuk app, which manages capacity in the Haramain.
Holders of a used US, UK or Schengen visa

Holders of valid US, UK or Schengen visas can also enter Saudi Arabia more easily. If your visa has already been used to enter the issuing country at least once, you can usually obtain a visa on arrival, and you may also be assessed for an eVisa in advance. Flying with a Saudi carrier and arriving by air are part of the conditions - we confirm the details for your exact case.

If you hold a US, UK or Schengen visit visa that you have already used for entry at least once, you may be assessed for a Saudi visa on arrival. Unused visas do not count, and the border decision is final - which is why this route suits confident, well-documented travellers.

If you hold one of the 72 eligible passports, the tourist eVisa is your route for holidays, events, visiting friends and family informally, and Umrah outside the Hajj season. Our eligibility page lists all 72 countries - and our country pages give the answer for every passport on earth.

Passport valid six months, residency valid three months, and the profession condition that used to block applications no longer applies. This is the route most UAE-based Pakistanis use, and it produces the standard one-year, multiple-entry tourist eVisa.

In the cities

In the cities, Saudi Arabia is close to a card-first country: contactless cards and phone payments are accepted in malls, restaurants, hotels, taxis booked by app and most shops, riding on the local mada network alongside the international card schemes. Carry a modest cash float anyway - small groceries, older taxis, market stalls and tips still run on notes, and a 100-riyal note solves problems a card cannot. ATMs are everywhere, including airport arrivals halls, and they give the bank rate; exchange kiosks at airports are convenient but rarely the best value. One setting worth knowing: when a card terminal offers to charge you in your home currency instead of riyals, choose riyals - the conversion offered at the till is almost always worse than your bank's.

Jeddah connections put you an hour from Al-Balad's coral-stone old town and the Red Sea corniche. Jeddah has been Makkah's port and pilgrim gateway for over 1,000 years

Jeddah has been a port for as long as there has been trade on the Red Sea, and the pilgrim gateway for Makkah for over a thousand years. That history made it the Kingdom's most outward-looking city - merchant families from across the Indian Ocean, a famous art scene, and a local saying that Jeddah is 'different'. The Corniche runs for miles along the sea, the old town is a UNESCO site, and the pace is set by the water. If Riyadh is the Kingdom's head, Jeddah is its smile.

Jeddah is the Kingdom's loose, coastal counterweight: Al-Balad's coral-stone tower houses and carved wooden balconies, the long Corniche with the King Fahd Fountain offshore, seafood at the centre of the table, and the Red Sea a few metres from the pavement. It is also the traditional gateway for pilgrims, which gives the city a cosmopolitan depth the capital is still growing into. Base here for the sea air and day-trip nowhere - Jeddah is the destination.

Plugs are Type G - the three rectangular pins used in the UK and the UAE - so visitors from Europe, the US and most of Asia need an adapter, ideally a universal one with USB ports. For emergencies, Riyadh, Makkah and the Eastern Province use the unified 911 number; elsewhere, 999 reaches the police and 997 an ambulance. The Saudi weekend is Friday and Saturday, which shifts opening hours more than visitors expect. And a few words of Arabic earn smiles everywhere: As-salamu alaykum (hello, literally 'peace be upon you'), Shukran (thank you), Min fadlik (please, to a man) and B'kam? (how much?). None of this takes long to arrange - an hour at the airport and in your first shop - and it quietly removes most of the friction from the trip that follows.

Ramadan countdown
Ramadan in Saudi Arabia

Ramadan is the month of fasting: from dawn to sunset, Muslims refrain from food and drink, and the rhythm of the Kingdom changes around it. Days are quieter, offices and shops often open later, and everything comes alive after sunset - iftar (the breaking of the fast) is a social feast, and the nights run long with prayers, markets and family gatherings.
Ramadan is the peak, followed by the winter school holidays. The quietest Umrah weeks are usually just after Hajj season and in the hottest months.
Ramadan moves about 11 days earlier each Gregorian year

Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier each year. Visiting then is a distinctive experience - quiet days, electric nights, iftar invitations - with daytime restaurant closures to plan around, and for Umrah pilgrims it is the most sought-after (and busiest) time of all. Hajj reverses the logic: the Hajj period brings pilgrim-only restrictions around Makkah, tourist eVisas are not the instrument for it, and the holy cities are effectively closed to ordinary tourism. Check the Hijri calendar before fixing dates - our converter on this site does exactly that.

Rijal Almaa's stone towers are edged with white quartz patterns

Rijal Almaa, the stone heritage village in the valley below Abha, is the postcard: multi-storey stone towers edged with white quartz patterns, once a trading post on the route between Yemen and the Hijaz. In Abha itself, the painted houses of the Muftaha art village and the cable cars dropping toward the lake fill an easy day. The Al Soudah parklands - juniper forest, picnic terraces, viewpoints that drop off the escarpment edge into cloud - are the weekend heart of the region.
Riyadh
Riyadh - also the Kingdom's largest city and its business heart.

Riyadh Season's Boulevard City is the capital showing off - themed zones, arenas, restaurants and crowds until late, running through the winter months. Around it, a coffee culture that rivals anywhere (speciality cafes are a genuine scene here), malls that function as evening social centres, and a restaurant range from Yemeni mandi houses to chef-led tasting menus. KAFD, the financial district's forest of towers, is worth an architectural wander even if finance leaves you cold.

Riyadh is vast, flat and organised on a grid: the historic core in the south (Ad Diriyah is actually a separate city to the north-west), the business towers along King Fahd Road in the middle, and the new developments pushing north. King Khalid International Airport sits about 35km north of the centre. The Riyadh Metro - six lines, opened in phases from late 2024 - has changed visitor logistics more than any single attraction; pair it with ride-hailing apps for the last mile and you can cross the city without a car.
Riyadh skyline
Riyadh to Jeddah is nearly 950 km - fly it or split it, don’t sprint it

Riyadh traffic is the country's real driving test: dense, fast and assertive at peak hours, with the metro now taking some of the strain. Jeddah is more forgiving; both cities reward patience, early lane choices and a navigation app with live traffic. Parking in central areas is mostly paid and app-based.

Riyadh's metro is new, fully air-conditioned and the easiest way across the city's distances - six lines linking the airport, financial district and main sights, paid by card or the Darb app. Ride-hailing apps (Uber and Careem) fill the gaps and are inexpensive by capital-city standards; allow real time for traffic at peak hours, because Riyadh is a big, car-shaped city.

Saudi Arabia entry points

Saudi Arabia has three mobile networks - STC, Mobily and Zain - and all three keep counters in the international arrivals halls of the major airports, usually open around the clock. Tourist SIM bundles pair a local number with a data allowance sized for a trip, and buying one takes a few minutes. You will need your passport: Saudi SIMs are registered to an identity document by law, and the staff will scan it and take a fingerprint on a small reader. That is normal, quick, and the reason unregistered street-corner SIMs are not a thing here. For coverage, STC is generally the widest across the country; inside the cities and along the main highways, all three are strong.

Saudi Arabia hosts one of the largest Bangladeshi communities in the world, and family visits run on sponsorship: your relative in the Kingdom obtains the approved family-visit invitation through the official channels, and you apply against it before travelling. Begin early, keep names and dates consistent across every document, and expect the host's paperwork to set the timeline.
Saudi Arabia in 7 Days: A First-Timer's Itinerary
Saudi Arabia in 7 Days: A First-Timer's Itinerary | Visit Saudi - visit-saudi.ae

Saudi Arabia is a monarchy, and uniquely among modern states it carries its ruling family's name: the Al Saud, whose first state was founded at Diriyah in 1744. The family is large - thousands of princes and princesses - but the line of kings runs through one man and his sons.

Saudi Arabia is big - Riyadh to AlUla alone is over 1,000 kilometres - so a good week is built on domestic flights, not highways. This itinerary runs in an arc: two nights in Riyadh, two in AlUla, three in Jeddah, flying between each and finishing by the Red Sea, close to an international airport for the way home. It works best between November and February, when the whole country is comfortably warm rather than split between pleasant cities and punishing heat. The tourist eVisa gives you up to 90 days in the Kingdom, so a week like this sits well inside a single stay - and because the visa is multiple-entry, you can also split the route across two shorter trips within the year.
Saudi Arabia is more relaxed for visitors than its reputation suggests - and a few simple habits still make every interaction smoother.
Saudi Arabia is more relaxed than its reputation and more traditional than its malls suggest. The customs that matter, explained without the scare stories.

Saudi Arabia is photogenic and mostly welcoming to cameras - landscapes, architecture and street scenes are fine. The rules are about people and security: ask before photographing individuals (especially women and families), and never photograph military sites, airports' security areas or government installations. Drones require permits; leave yours at home unless you have arranged one.

Saudi Arabia occupies most of the Arabian Peninsula - a land of gravel plains and sand seas, volcanic highlands in the west, and the green terraces of Asir in the south-west. It is the birthplace of Islam and home to its two holiest cities, Makkah and Madinah, which welcome millions of pilgrims every year.

Saudi Arabia opened the eVisa to residents of all six GCC countries. If you live in the UAE on a valid residence permit, you can apply online on the strength of that residency - your nationality does not need to be on the 72-country list, and your profession no longer decides anything.

Saudi Arabia requires visitors to hold medical insurance for their trip. On the eVisa route this is not something you arrange separately: the official fee includes the mandatory medical policy, and the policy is issued alongside your visa by the appointed insurer. It is one of the reasons the official fee is what it is - you are paying for a visa and a medical policy together.

Saudi Arabia runs a dedicated route for people who live in the Gulf. If you are a legal resident of a GCC country - the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain or Oman - you can apply for the Saudi tourist eVisa on the strength of that residency, whatever passport you hold. An Indian, Pakistani, Filipino or Egyptian passport that could not apply on its own qualifies through a Gulf residency.

Saudi Arabia runs on cards and phone payments in the cities, with a small cash float for taxis, tips and market stalls - our money and SIM guide has the full picture, including the tourist SIMs sold in the arrivals hall and the fixed 3.75 exchange rate that makes riyal prices easy to read. Power is the other quiet essential: a Type G adapter (the three-pin UK style), a power bank for the long days, and a multi-port charger if you are travelling as a family. Download offline maps of Makkah and Madinah before you go; hotel Wi-Fi is strong, but the streets around the Haram at prayer times test any network.

Saudi Arabia treats a US, UK or Schengen visa as evidence that another strict system has already vetted you. If you hold one - and it is the right kind, in the right state - you qualify for a simplified route into the Kingdom even when your passport alone is not on the 72-country eVisa list. For many Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Filipino and Egyptian travellers working in the Gulf or travelling widely, this is the door that opens Saudi tourism.

Saudi Arabia uses Type G plugs - the three-pin British style, same as the UAE and UK - so most Gulf and British travellers need no adapter; everyone else should pack one. Add a power bank (long desert days), serious sun protection, a refillable bottle, and any prescription medicines IN their original packaging with the prescription itself: some common medicines elsewhere are controlled here, and the paperwork is the difference between a non-event and a problem. Our prohibited-items guide covers the sensitive categories.
Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast: the Dammam-Khobar-Dhahran tri-city, corniches and Half Moon Bay, the King Fahd Causeway to Bahrain, and Ithra - the cultural centre that changed the region.

Saudi Arabia's currency is the riyal (SAR), divided into 100 halalas. Unusually for travellers, the exchange rate is a fixed point rather than a moving target: the riyal is pegged to the US dollar at 3.75 to the dollar, and has been for decades. That makes mental arithmetic easy - divide riyal prices by four for a rough dollar figure, or by roughly five for pounds - and our free currency converter will turn any price into your own currency exactly. Notes run from 1 to 500 riyals; the 100 and 500 are the ones to recognise, and coins appear for small change.

Saudi Arabia's open-air museum: Nabataean tombs older than Petra's fame, a rock shaped like an elephant, a mirrored concert hall in the desert - and how to plan days that do it justice.

Saudi Arabia's own visa system has modernised fast - the official KSA Visa platform, the MOFA portal and the tourist eVisa site are well built. What they cannot do is look at your photo and tell you it will be rejected, or notice that the name on your invitation does not match your passport. That human check is our job.

Saudi Arabia's public holidays are fewer and more concentrated than in most countries. Two are fixed to the Gregorian calendar: Founding Day on 22 February, marking the first Saudi state in 1727, and National Day on 23 September, marking the Kingdom's unification in 1932. The other two are the great religious festivals of the Islamic year: Eid al-Fitr, which ends Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha, the festival of the sacrifice, which falls during the Hajj season and includes the Day of Arafat. Between them, these four shape the country's working year far more than any others.

Saudi Arabia's stopover programme turns a connection into a short trip. When you book a flight through Saudi Arabia with Saudia or flynas, a transit visa for 48 or 96 hours can be issued alongside the ticket. It is designed for exactly this: one booking, one short stay, then onward travel.

Saudi Vision 2030 in plain English: its three themes, the tourism targets, the giga-projects, and what the transformation means for your trip.

Saudi Vision 2030 is the Kingdom's national transformation plan, launched in April 2016 by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman under King Salman. Its premise is simple: a country this rich in oil, location and young people should not depend on oil alone. The plan sets hundreds of targets across the economy and society, delivered through programmes and giga-projects funded largely by the Public Investment Fund.

That single principle answers most situations a tourist will meet, and it is also simply practical clothing for the climate - loose cotton and linen are what the heat asks for anyway. Saudi etiquette for visitors

Saudi food has a meat-heavy reputation - all that kabsa and grilled lamb - but the everyday table is built on dishes that happen to be vegetarian or vegan: falafel, fuul (slow-cooked fava beans), hummus, moutabel, tabbouleh, fattoush, lentil soup, olives, dates and endless Arabic coffee. Breakfast in particular is a gift: a traditional spread of fuul, eggs, cheese, olives, halawa and tamis bread is mostly vegetarian before you have asked for anything special. Our Saudi food guide covers the classics; this one is about navigating them without meat.

Saudi hospitality is not a marketing line - expect coffee and dates offered in shops, offices and homes, and accept with your right hand. A few Arabic greetings go a long way: 'As-salamu alaykum' on meeting, 'Shukran' for thanks. Friday is the main day of rest, and business hours compress in Ramadan, when eating and drinking in public during daylight is avoided out of respect for those fasting.

Saudi law is strict, publicly enforced, and applies to visitors exactly as it applies to residents. Alcohol is prohibited outright, and drug offences carry severe penalties - never carry anything for anyone else. Photograph people only with their permission, and do not photograph military or government installations. Public behaviour is expected to stay modest: dress as our dress code guide describes, keep affection between couples discreet, and avoid loud arguments or gestures in public - the argument you win on the street can still cost you the day. None of this is hard to follow; it simply rewards knowing it before you land rather than after.

Saudis travel for the holidays, in numbers that transform the domestic map. Makkah and Madinah fill completely around Eid al-Fitr, when the whole country wants to be in the holy cities; Eid al-Adha coincides with Hajj, when access to Makkah is managed for pilgrims alone. Start where the Kingdom started: Diriyah, on Riyadh's north-western edge, whose mud-brick At-Turaif district is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the original home of the Saudi royal family. Give it a morning, then balance it with the National Museum for the story of the peninsula in one building, and the Masmak Fortress in the old city. On the second day, go modern: the Kingdom Centre's Sky Bridge at dusk for the whole city laid out below, and an evening among the boulevards and restaurants of the new districts. Riyadh rewards one slow day and one full one - do not try to compress it into a stopover.

The Corniche and the sea

The Corniche is Jeddah's living room: sculpture-dotted promenades (the city has collected major open-air art for decades), the King Fahd Fountain - at over 300 metres, the tallest of its kind in the world, lit at night - and families out until late. Al Rahma Mosque, the 'floating mosque', sits on pillars over the water at high tide. For the sea itself, the private beach clubs north in Obhur Al Janoubia are where Jeddah swims, and dive boats run to reefs that justify the Red Sea's reputation all on their own.

The Eastern Province is standard Saudi tourism on your eVisa. One specific caution: the causeway to Bahrain is a border crossing - leaving for Bahrain ends that Saudi stay, and coming back uses another entry on a multiple-entry visa (or needs a new visa if yours is single-entry). Plan the day trip with that in mind, and keep your passport - not just your Gulf residency card - with you.

The Eastern Province runs on the tri-city sprawl of Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran along the Arabian Gulf. Dammam is the working port and provincial capital; Khobar is the polished Corniche city of cafes and malls; Dhahran is the Aramco city, home to King Fahd University and the region's landmark cultural building. Together they feel different from Riyadh or Jeddah - a Gulf port culture of seafronts, seafood and weekend causeway traffic.

The Saudi tourist eVisa can be applied for entirely online by passport holders of 72 countries across North and South America, Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania - including the United States, United Kingdom, all EU states, China, Japan, Australia and South Africa. The visa is valid for one year, allows multiple entries, and permits stays of up to 90 days per visit.

The Saudi tourist eVisa is issued in two shapes. The standard version is valid for one year, allows multiple entries, and permits stays of up to 90 days per visit. The other version is a single-entry visa with a stay of up to 30 days. Both are applied for the same way, through the same application - the system issues the version your passport qualifies for.

Three traps catch vegetarians here. Rice is the big one: the fragrant rice under many dishes is often cooked in meat stock or finished with samna (clarified butter), so 'just the rice' is not automatically vegetarian - ask. Soups can be built on chicken stock even when they look like pure lentil. And 'vegetable' dishes in smaller restaurants sometimes share oil or a grill with meat, which matters to some and not to others. None of this is said to discourage: it is said so you ask the two questions that settle it, because kitchens here are generally happy to adjust when the request is clear.
